title: Liquid Crystals
textbookText: Liquid Crystals Liquid crystals are a unique state of matter, between solid (crystalline) and liquid (isotropic) phases some compounds form a distinct, different intermediate phase, sometimes referred to as the “fourth state of matter” or “mesophase”. These compounds display properties of both solid and liquid. Certain solids on heating undergo two sharp phase transformations; firstly they fuse to turbid liquid and then at higher temperature converted into a clear liquid. The turbid/ translucent state is called liquid crystals / mesomorphic state.

Solid—-----------> liquid crystal—----------------->clear liquid state The liquid crystals show anisotropy i.e. they have different physical properties in different directions. Also they exhibit double refraction and give interference patterns in polarized light. Thus the structures of liquid crystal are in between of liquid and a crystalline solid. They show properties of liquids like mobility, surface tension, viscosity etc. and optical properties of crystalline solids. e.g. p-azoxy anisole, p-azoxyphenetole,Cholestryl benzoate etc The study of Liquid crystal started in year 1888 AD by Austrian scientist Friedrich Reinitizer.
The liquid crystals can be classified on the basis of their structure or molecular arrangement into 3 types: Smectic liquid crystals. Nematic liquid crystals & Chloesteric liquid crystals.

(a) Smectic (Greek: = Soap- like) liquid crystals: (1) These have molecules parallel to each other arranged in layers. The smectic state is exhibited by common soaps at higher temperature ~ 200 oC in the presence of water. (2) The smectic liquid crystals do not flow like normal liquids. They have limited mobility. (3) They flow in layers and the distribution of velocity is different in different layers i.e. the flow of smectic liquid crystals is non-Newtonian. The viscosity concept is not applicable to these crystals. (4) The smectic liquid crystals give X-ray diffraction patterns like solid crystals but in one direction only. e.g. ethyl- p- azoxy benzoate, ethyl- p- azoxy cinnamate etc.
